newsitem.title: INDIA: India shipping sees little relief in budget.
newsitem.headline: India shipping sees little relief in budget.

text.p: Indian shipping firms, facing stiff competition from foreign rivals, have sought tax incentives from this week's national budget but analysts said on Thursday the relief might fall short of expectations.

"We have asked for tax reliefs to seafarers, and a full tax exemption for funds reserved for buying ships among other things," Indian National Shipowners' Association (INSA) chief executive B.V. Nilkund said on Thursday.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram presents the budget for the 1997/98 fiscal year beginning on April 1 to parliament at 5 p.m. (1130 GMT) on Friday.
INSA has asked the Finance Ministry for authority to borrow more money in overseas markets and for recognition as an essential infrastructure industry, which entails tax benefits.

"Shipping should be recognised as an essential infrastructure and 100 percent service export industry, and fiscal benefits should be provided to it as are made available to similar sectors," said INSA president B.L. Mehta.
"This will ensure that Indian shipping is not disadvantaged vis-a-vis foreign flag competition."
Ports and power generation are among sectors which are recognised as essential infrastructure industries and thus entitled to special tax benefits.
Mehta said other seafaring countries offered soft loans, lower or zero corporate tax and exemption from income tax to shipping companies.
"Shipping has thrived where the flag countries have exempted shipping profits from tax or provided special tax relief for shipping companies," he said.

According to INSA, Indian ships' share of the country's overseas trade fell to 28.7 percent in 1994/95 from 33 percent in the previous year. Figures for 1995/96 and the latest period were not available.
Mehta said restoration of a 100 percent tax exemption for funds used for buying ships was essential for fleet expansion. The exemption was scaled down to 50 percent in 1994/95.
Mehta called for tax exemption for seafarers to deter them from joining foreign ships that offered tax-free pay packets.
Highly capital intensive, shipping firms require large amounts of money, both as equity and debt, to overhaul their fleets which can become obsolete quickly, he said.
According to INSA, India's existing fleet stands at 7.05 million gross registered tons (grt) and is targeted to expand to 9.0 million in the next five years.
An expansion plan seeks to add a new fleet of 2.0 million grt and replace 1.7 million grt, at a cost of 1.45 trillion rupees ($4.0 billion).
Analysts said India's shipping faced the prospect of negative growth due to financial constraints on fleet expansion.
The shipping industry is also demanding that it be allowed to raise $700 million annually to buy ships against $500 million permitted at present.

"I don't think the budget will make any special allocation in regard to commercial borrowings," said Elsy Abraham, an analyst with foreign securities firm James Capel. "In the past they have not been able to use $500 million in a year."

P.R. Naware, an official of Great Eastern Shipping Co, said he hoped the rate of depreciation on ships would be raised to 40 percent -- the current rate for road transport and airlines -- from 20 percent. "We are expecting some tax reliefs, but nothing dramatic," Naware added.
